name: Pushbullet
tagline: Sends links, files, and notifications between your phone, tablet, and desktop.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The part people use most, shove a link or a file from one device to another and have it show up instantly, is a small server, a database, and a web push subscription. An agent can build that in a sitting and it will work fine across any device with a modern browser. What it cannot build in one shot is the half that made Pushbullet distinctive: mirroring Android notifications to your desktop and replying to SMS from a keyboard. That needs a signed native Android app using NotificationListenerService and SMS permissions, a Play Store listing or sideloading discipline, and a battery-friendly background channel. So you get the pipe, not the phone integration.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted relay where any logged-in device can push text, links, or files to your other devices, delivered live via web push and a running feed.
requirements: A small always-on host or VPS with HTTPS, because web push needs a real certificate
VAPID keys for web push, stored in .env
Disk or object storage for pushed files
A browser on each device, or a native Android build if you want notification mirroring
whatYouLose: Android notification mirroring to the desktop, which needs a native app and permissions you cannot fake in a browser
Sending and replying to SMS from your computer
Polished native apps on every platform, including the share sheet and clipboard integrations
Reliable background delivery on iOS, where web push is fussy and easily evicted
Universal copy-paste sync and remote file browsing on your phone
moatNotes: The moat is not the relay, it is the platform-level hooks: notification listeners, SMS APIs, share sheets, and the app store trust needed to ask for them.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the interesting features are the ones that live inside the operating system, not on a server. Reading your notifications and sending your texts requires a signed app that has already fought Android's permission model and Apple's background rules, and most people would rather pay a few dollars than maintain sideloaded builds on three devices. The paid tier also removes size and message limits that are boring but real once you actually use the thing daily.
notes: The link and file pipe is a one-sitting build; the phone side is the whole product for anyone who used it for SMS.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted cross-device push relay called Relay. Single project, no accounts service, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Node 20 with TypeScript, Fastify, SQLite via better-sqlite3, server-rendered HTML with a small vanilla JS client, plain CSS. No React, no Next, no ORM.

What it does:
1. Single-user auth: one shared password from .env, session cookie signed with a secret from .env. No signup flow.
2. Devices: each browser that logs in registers itself with a name and a Web Push subscription. Store devices in SQLite. Allow renaming and deleting devices.
3. Pushes: a form and a POST /api/push endpoint accepting type note, link, or file. Text and links are stored as rows. Files upload via multipart to a local uploads directory with a configurable max size, served back through an authenticated route.
4. Delivery: on every push, send a Web Push notification to all subscribed devices except the origin device, using VAPID keys from .env and the web-push library. Notification click opens the push in the feed. Also push live updates to any open tab over Server-Sent Events.
5. Feed: reverse-chronological list of pushes with copy-to-clipboard for text and links, download for files, delete per item, and a clear-all. Paginate at 50.
6. CLI: a small script, npm run push -- "some text", that posts to the server using a token from .env, so you can pipe from a terminal.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: Android notification mirroring, SMS sending, native mobile apps, end-to-end encryption, multi-user sharing, FCM.

Requirements: all secrets in .env with a .env.example, no hardcoded keys. Include a script to generate VAPID keys. Ship a Dockerfile and a docker-compose.yml with a volume for the SQLite file and uploads. README must state that Web Push requires HTTPS and that iOS needs the site installed to the home screen. Include a manifest.json and service worker so it installs as a PWA. Seed nothing. Make it work with npm install, npm run dev.
